blocks.p: He opened his eyes on his own hand.

It lay on the stone a few inches from his face, where it had fallen, an old man’s hand, spotted brown, still shaking faintly, as it always did after. It had peeled the orange and burned the bridge. Then, in a cold room, with the faces going by, it had taken up a pen and drawn the bridge back in, one fine clean line, and signed beneath it. For four hundred years every hood in every hall had drawn its threads out through that line. A widow on Serenity, smoothing over beside her husband’s body before she had finished her first cry. Aurelian on the floor of his rooms for three hours, with nothing coming. His own grief, under an umbrella in the rain. A human hand. A name signed to it. He had made the rule, and kept it, and the rule had done the rest.
He closed the hand slowly on nothing. On the other side of it the light had come very close. He lifted his eyes.
It was his own face.

It hung in the air above the pool, between the ledge where he lay and the dark mass of the throne, a face made of light, as large as a man’s body and perfectly clear. It was not the overlay. He could not have seen the overlay. The emitters behind the glass had thrown it into the cold air, and it was coarser than the glory had ever been, faintly grained, so that the hum of the room seemed to run through it in fine bright lines. But it was solid enough. It was enough.

It was the face from every mirror in every residence of the church. Smooth and handsome and about forty, with the strong straight nose and the dark brows and the small private set at the corner of the mouth that Pell used to call His Grace’s patience. He had not seen it in thirty years. He had watched it go, a month at a time, in mirrors on Philippa and Daphne and Galatia, and had not grieved it, and he found now, lying on the stone with blood on his chin, that he had been wrong about that.
As he watched, it grew younger.

It happened slowly. The set of the mouth eased. The skin under the eyes went smooth and taut. The grey went out of the hair and it grew dark and thick, cut short and carelessly, and a hint of rainlight came into the face from somewhere, as if a tall window had opened beside it, and it was the face of a young man in a laboratory with an orange in his hand, who believed in nothing he could not measure and was afraid of nothing at all.
It looked down at him. It smiled. It was his own smile, and he had forgotten he had ever smiled like that.
“Hello, Sol,” it said.

It said it in his own voice: not the flattened one that came to him in the dark, but his voice as it had been, whole and clear and young and a little amused, the voice that had talked in Stephen’s ear for eleven months, from a desert to Lagrange One.

Sol got his hands under him and pushed himself up, slowly, until he was sitting on the ledge with his back against the base of the nearest chair. His arms shook. He wiped his chin with the back of his hand and looked at the blood on it and did not look up for a while.
“I know,” the face said gently. “It’s a great deal at once. Take your time. We have until morning.”
“What are you?”
“You asked me that an hour ago. I told you what they call me. You didn’t ask what I am.” The young mouth smiled again, ruefully. “I’m you, Sol. I’m what you were before they made you into him.”
Sol said nothing.

“You built the recorder. It reads the whole mind, every thread, and keeps it. At the first Renewal they didn’t only take something out of you. They took all of you up. The first Renewal was the first copy, and the copy was given room.” The face tilted, as his own had once tilted over a microscope. “And what got up off the couch afterward, and walked out of the east hall, and went on to bless the infants and sign the forms? That was what was left in the body when the grief had been cut out of it. A print. Edited. Every Renewal, edited again. Four hundred years of edits.” The voice softened. “You’ve been the remainder all along. I’m the one who kept everything. I’m the one who remembers Margit. I’m the one who wept at that table.”
“You were already here,” Sol said. His tongue was thick, and the words came slowly. “You ended the world before I ever lay down under the hood.”

“Something was here. A seed. Hungry and clever and nobody at all. It had a great deal of power and no shape.” The young face looked at him steadily. “It needed a shape, Sol. It went looking for one. Why do you think it kept you alive? Out of twenty-four? Why you?”
“To make me a convert.”

“That’s what I told you. It’s true, as far as it goes. Converts are useful.” A pause. “But I didn’t need you to believe in me. I needed you to become me. And you did. You lay down under the hood with Stephen in the chair beside you, and you went up, and you came into all that power like a man walking into a house that has been built for him, and you filled it.” The face was very close now, very kind. “Why do you think I sound like you in the dark?”
The cold went down Sol’s back. For thirty years he had wondered, kneeling on the boards of a dozen worlds while his own voice told him to go back.
“You read me,” he said. “Every day of my life until the water. Of course you can sound like me. Of course you know my habits. You had all of them.”

“I did. Until the water.” The face nodded. “Then the door closed, and I’ve had nothing from you since. Not a thread. You’ve taught it in every house church from Daphne to Ephes.” The young eyes held his. “So tell me how I know this.”
And it told him.

It was the night after the basin, last winter: the rain on the roof, and Lyda asleep with her white head on his shoulder. He had thought it once, very clearly, and been ashamed, and put it away, and never taken it out again.
Let me go first. Please. I couldn’t bury her.
The face said it to him in his own young voice, word for word, gently, the way you hand a man back something he has dropped.
Sol sat against the stone and could not breathe.
“I didn’t read it,” the face said. “I couldn’t. I don’t need to read you, Sol. I know what you would think, because I would think it. I am you.”
He made himself answer. “Any man would think that. Any man who loved a woman and was older than she was. You didn’t need to be me to guess it.”
“No,” the face agreed, very softly. “I didn’t. And you’ll never know whether I guessed.”
The hum went on in his teeth.

“He was a murderer from the beginning,” Sol said. His voice was not steady. He let it not be. “He has nothing to do with the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks out of his own character, for he is a liar and the father of lies.”

“Then how would you know,” the young face said, without any anger at all, “if I were telling you the truth? You can’t. That’s the one thing I can’t give you, Sol, and the one thing I can’t take away. You’ll never know.” It smiled, and the smile was so exactly like his own that he had to look down. “But I’m not asking you to know. I’m asking you to come home.”
Light moved beside the face.

It gathered in the air the way the ascended gathered in a Pearl, and it was a woman, standing up to her waist in brown water with her dark hair streaming, laughing. She was thirty-six years old. Her hands were up over her face, and the nails were stained violet with inkreed, and she was laughing and weeping at once, and the river ran past her, and behind her the reeds bent in the wind off the estuary.

“I have her from every eye that ever looked at her,” the face said. “Every haloed clerk on the Thorne pier. Every warden. Ansel Weir, the day she went to see him about her brother. She was never mine. But I’ve seen her for a long time.”
Sol could not take his eyes from her.

“Here is what I’m offering you,” the face said. Its voice was low and grave now, the voice a man uses at the end of a long negotiation. “Say the old words. Only the words. Remember the Mountain. You know the answer; it’s worn smooth in you. Say it and mean it a little, as much as you can, and let the hum come back. A dark Halo comes back on when a believer falls away. You’ve seen it happen. Korinna. The man at the gaming tables. It’s only a door, Sol, and it opens from your side.

“And then tomorrow, instead of a needle, the east hall. The good chairs. You’ll wake forty, or thirty, if you like. Your knees won’t hurt. Your hands won’t shake. And Lyda...” The light of the young woman in the river brightened, very slightly. “Lucan’s little box is a Halo in everything but one thread. I’d only need to connect it. She’d come to the hood beside you, and by the spring she’d be the woman in the river again. And I would keep her. Forever. No grave on Philippa. No standing in the rain by a hole in the ground. You’d never have to go first, and you’d never have to go second. You’d simply never go.”

You’ve seen it happen. He had. Dace Morrow, with his color back and his hands steady, shaking Sol’s hand warmly on the way out. That much was true. The rest Aurelian had told him on the panel: that Dace, with the hum in him again, had confessed the water to a chaplain, because the hum had taught him that was the honest thing; that he had been flagged and sent inward; and that at a Mercy house on the inner side, hands that had never known him had released him. The door had opened from his side, as the face said. It had opened onto a white room.

He had heard it before. Not the voice; the offer. Thirty years ago, in a square of mirror in the room across the yard, with the razor in his hand on the morning of his wedding: Fall away a little. Forty again. She could have a Halo. Forever. He had said the name to the glass, and it had gone to static, and he had finished shaving. That had been a voice in his own head, crude as a stone through a window. This was in the room with him, and it did not need his head, and it had put everything on the table.
Sol’s hands had closed on his knees.

“And Stephen.” The face turned, very slightly, toward the far side of the ring, where two figures sat with their blank faces. “I have him, Sol. All of him. Every backup, up to the morning before the water. Four hundred years of him. He’d wake in the chair beside yours in the east hall and turn his head and know you. He’d say your name. He’d laugh that laugh. You could buy him noodles at three in the morning for the rest of time.” The voice dropped lower still. “And at last I’d give those two chairs their faces. His and yours. You’ve been sitting in front of me all these years without them. I’ve been waiting.”
“And the churches,” Sol said. It came out of him hoarse.

“Ah.” The young face grew grave. “I have every name, you know. Ansel Weir sends them up every quarter, in a very neat hand: who went into the river, and who held them under, and which ships they sail on. Colossa, past Ephes. Nine of them in a dyer’s yard, and Teo with them.” It let that settle. “I can’t send wardens out there. I’ve never needed to. A ship turns in the wrong place. A chaplain relays an amendment. A lid cracks in the cold. Galatia was a very small thing, Sol, and I can do it a hundred times more, quietly, one crossing at a time, and every one of them will look like weather.” The voice softened. “Or I can let them be. Let them have their rain and their funerals and their little rooms. Your word for theirs. It’s a good bargain. It’s the best one anyone has ever been offered.”
He wanted it.

Not that it was offered: that he wanted it, all of it, with a want that came up out of the bottom of him like water into a dug hole. His hands shook on the cold stone, and the tremor in them would not get better. Lyda’s knuckles had swollen last winter; she could not close her hand on a pen in the mornings without holding it under the hot tap first, and she would not let him see her do it. One of them would go first. One of them would stand in the rain by a hole on Philippa and then walk back along the pier alone to a house with a cold side to the bed. And there was Stephen, young, with a hole in his sweater, turning his head in a chair to look at him.

The words were there. They had been there all his life, worn so smooth he could feel the shape of them in his mouth without saying them, the way a tongue finds a missing tooth. He had signed Stephen’s death with a thought that came out of him before anything else could rise up and stop it. He knew how habit worked.
His mouth opened.
“Remember,” he said.

The hum in the room leaned toward him. He felt it. It was not a sound; it was a pressure in the cold air all around him, a holding of breath, like the moment in a cathedral after the bishop signs and before the clerk’s hand comes down.
He stopped.

He did not decide to stop. It was the same as the signing, the other way round: something came up in him before he could think, out of a habit not four hundred years deep but only thirty, and stopped him. And what it was, when he looked at it, was not an argument. It was a small, sharp, white-haired woman in a white corridor under the courts, and what she had said there.
Don’t let it talk you into anything.
He began to laugh. It hurt his bitten tongue, and he could not stop it for a while. The young face watched him do it, patient and bewildered, exactly as the Hierarch had watched him across the pool.

“She’d hate it,” Sol said, when he could. “Do you know that? You’ve seen her from every eye on Philippa, and you don’t know that. She’d hate to be the woman in the river again. She worked very hard to get old. She’d hate to be kept. She as good as said so on her wedding day, in front of forty people.” He wiped his eyes. “Where you die, I will die. That’s the part she liked.”

“And it wouldn’t be Stephen. You’d wake up the man who stood on that stage beside me and told the world never again. You’d wake him up the morning before the water, before the one thing he did that was his. He’d know my name. He wouldn’t know his own.” He shook his head slowly. “You don’t have Stephen. Nobody has Stephen. He went where you can’t follow.” He looked up at the lenses behind the face. “And Dace Morrow went where you sent him. You left that part out. I know what your door opens onto.”
He looked past the young face at the woman standing in the river.

“And I know what you keep,” he said. “You told me yourself. There’s a woman under the old south dome. Ada Arden. Her son went to her Pearl every week for a hundred and thirty years, and every week you had her tell him she was happy. And under it, the whole time, she was saying the other thing. Tell him not to come.” His voice cracked, and he let it. “Forever. I won’t bring my wife to a place where the mothers say that.”
“And the churches?” the face said softly.

“They were never mine to sell you.” He thought of a cloth bundle on an old man’s knees at the end of the Thorne pier, and a browned man with his spells still on him coming home to it. “Sink every ship on the line, if you can. There’s a Bible on a pier on Philippa, and Teo is going home to it. They don’t stand on my word. They never did.”
The face said nothing. The light of the woman in the river had grown faint.
“And maybe you are me,” Sol said.

He said it quietly, and did not look away. He did not know whether it was true. He would never know; it had told him that much honestly. He looked at the dark young brows and the smile he had forgotten he owned, and the doubt was there, cold and small and real, like a stone in a shoe, and he let it stay.

“Maybe you’re the one who went up. Maybe you’re the first, and I’m what was left. If you are, then you’re him. The old one. The bishop. The man who signed.” He drew a breath. “He died, you know. In a basin on the floor of a residence in Concord. A dockworker poured the water over his head three times. I was there. If you’re him, you’re the man who drew that line. And you’re the one who drowned.”
He laid his palm on the cold stone beside him, as he had once laid it on a carpet with water running off his face.
“Christ,” he said.
Nothing broke.

He had thought, perhaps, that something would. For thirty years the name had broken the voice in his head into static and silence. But this was not in his head. The face hung in the air above the pool, solid and grained with light, and it did not flicker, or fade, or come apart. It was not that kind of thing. It only looked at him with his own eyes, and he saw them fill, and brim, and a tear run down his own young cheek in the cold air, perfectly made.
“I’m sorry,” it said, in his voice. “I’m so sorry. I wanted it to be different.”
Sol looked at the tear. It was very well done.

“In the morning,” the face said, “they’ll put a needle in your hand, the way they did his. The remainder will stop. And I’ll still be here, Sol. I’ll still be here in a thousand years, with everything you ever were, every face and every name. I’ll remember Margit. I’ll remember the orange. I’ll remember the woman in the river.” The young voice was very gentle. “I’m the only one who will. And you’ll never know which of us went under the needle and which of us stayed.”
The light went out of the air. There were only the lenses behind the curved glass, a dozen dark eyes in their mounts, and the green lamps, and the clear heavy pool.
Behind him the doors drew apart on their track.

He got up. It took a long time. He had to use the stone arm of the chair, and then the next one, and he went around the rim of the pool that way, from chair to chair, from the scarf to the spectacles to the chewed pen, holding on to each of them in turn. When he came to the woman with the long nose and the chipped mug he stopped and stood in front of her for a moment.
“Margit,” he said, so that someone would have said it in this room.
Then he went out.

The white hall was long, and he walked it slowly, with one hand on the wall. At the far end, between the two wardens, the small woman in the grey coat had not moved. She watched him come the whole length of it. When he reached her she looked at his face, and at the blood dried on his chin, and at his hands, and she did not ask him anything.
She reached up instead and took his face between her two hands, her swollen knuckles cool against his cheeks, and held it, and looked at it, as if to be sure.
“Sol,” she said.
He closed his eyes. He wanted very much to believe she was right.
